phase-change-energy-s1.title: Heating curve of Compound Q
phase-change-energy-s1.text: A 47.05 g sample of solid Compound Q (molar mass 94.10 g/mol) at 20.0 °C is heated by a heater that supplies 150. J of energy to the sample each second. Melting runs from 9.6 s to 47.2 s; boiling runs from 142.3 s to 295.3 s.

phase-change-energy-s2.title: Phase-change data for four substances
phase-change-energy-s2.text: Each enthalpy is measured at the normal melting or boiling point.

items.q: During which time interval is Compound Q entirely liquid?
options: From 47.2 s to 142.3 s
From 9.6 s to 47.2 s
From 142.3 s to 295.3 s
From 0 s to 9.6 s

why.correct: Sloped parts show one phase warming; flat parts show two phases changing at constant temperature. The liquid alone is the slope between the two flat parts.
options: Right: melting has finished at the end of the first flat part, and boiling has not yet begun.
This flat part is melting: solid and liquid are both present.
This flat part is boiling: liquid and gas are both present.
Before the first flat part, the sample is a solid warming up.

items.q: Calculate the molar enthalpy of fusion of Compound Q, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: that is kJ per gram. Divide by moles (mass ÷ molar mass) for a molar enthalpy.
Value: you used the time from 0 s to the end of melting. The energy for melting is only the flat part, 9.6 s to 47.2 s.

why.correct: Melting time = 47.2 s − 9.6 s = 37.6 s. Energy = 37.6 s × 150. J/s = 5640 J = 5.64 kJ. Moles = 47.05 g ÷ 94.10 g/mol = 0.500 mol. ΔHfus = 5.64 kJ ÷ 0.500 mol = 11.28 → 11.3 kJ/mol.

items.q: The boiling plateau is about four times as long as the melting plateau. Which explanation is correct?
options: Boiling breaks the covalent bonds inside the molecules of Compound Q; melting leaves them intact.
The temperature is higher during boiling, so each molecule needs more energy to move.
Boiling pulls the molecules almost fully apart; melting just loosens their attractions.
There is more liquid than solid in the sample, so boiling takes longer.

why.correct: Melting turns a fixed arrangement into a liquid where molecules still touch; vaporizing pulls them apart into a gas. More attractions are overcome, so ΔHvap > ΔHfus.
options: No covalent bonds break in either change; the molecules are still Compound Q in the gas.
The plateau length measures energy to overcome attractions, not the temperature.
Right: in the liquid, molecules still touch and attract; boiling overcomes nearly all those attractions.
The same 0.500 mol of Compound Q melts and then boils.

items.q: Between 142.3 s and 295.3 s, what happens to the average kinetic energy of the molecules of Compound Q?
options: It increases, because the heater keeps adding 150. J of energy to the sample each second.
It decreases, because the molecules spread far apart from each other as they become a gas.
It increases, because covalent bonds break and release energy.
It stays the same, because the energy goes into overcoming attractions between molecules.

why.correct: Temperature tracks average kinetic energy. On a flat part, the added energy separates molecules (potential energy goes up) while their average speed stays constant.
options: The energy is added, but it does not speed the molecules up while the temperature is flat.
Spreading out raises their potential energy; their average speed stays the same at constant temperature.
No covalent bonds break, and breaking bonds would absorb energy, not release it.
Right: constant temperature means constant average kinetic energy; the energy raises the potential energy.

items.q: Use the sloped part for the liquid to calculate the specific heat of liquid Compound Q, in J/(g·°C).

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by moles. Specific heat is per gram: divide by the mass, 47.05 g.
Value: you used the final temperature as ΔT. ΔT = 182.0 °C − 41.0 °C.

items.q: Methane, ammonia and water have similar molar masses, yet water's ΔHvap is about five times methane's. Which explanation is best?
options: Water has the larger molar mass of the two, so its molecules need more energy to escape from the liquid.
Water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds; methane molecules just by weaker London dispersion forces.
Water's O–H bonds are stronger than methane's C–H bonds, and those covalent bonds break when water boils.
Water boils at a higher temperature, and a higher temperature makes ΔHvap larger.

why.correct: ΔHvap measures the energy to separate molecules. With similar masses, the type of attraction decides: hydrogen bonding (water) ≫ London dispersion only (methane).
options: The molar masses (18.02 and 16.04 g/mol) are nearly the same, so mass cannot explain a fivefold difference.
Right: overcoming hydrogen bonds takes far more energy than overcoming the weak dispersion forces between small CH₄ molecules.
Boiling does not break covalent bonds; the gas is still H₂O molecules.
The higher boiling point and the larger ΔHvap have the same cause, stronger attractions; one does not cause the other.

items.q: How much energy, in kJ, is needed to vaporize 25.0 g of ethanol at its boiling point?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied grams by kJ/mol. Convert grams to moles first.
Value: you used ΔHfus. Vaporizing a liquid needs ΔHvap.

items.q: What is the energy change, in kJ, of 10.0 g of ammonia gas that condenses to liquid at −33.3 °C?

mistakes.why: Sign: condensing releases energy, so the ammonia's energy change is negative.
Value: convert grams to moles before multiplying by kJ/mol.

why.correct: n = 10.0 g ÷ 17.03 g/mol = 0.5872 mol. Condensing is the reverse of vaporizing, so q = −n × ΔHvap = −0.5872 mol × 23.3 kJ/mol = −13.68 → −13.7 kJ. The ammonia releases energy.

items.q: Which statements are supported by the data in the table? Select all that apply.
options: For each substance, more energy is needed to vaporize a mole than to melt a mole.
Ammonia molecules attract each other more strongly than ethanol molecules do.
A larger molar mass gives a larger ΔHfus.
Melting 1 mol of ice absorbs more energy than boiling 1 mol of liquid ammonia.

why.correct: Read the table row by row and column by column; reject a claim that one row breaks (ethanol's ΔHfus) or that the data contradict (ammonia vs ethanol).
options: Every ΔHvap in the table is larger than the ΔHfus in the same row.
Ammonia's ΔHvap (23.3 kJ/mol) and boiling point are both lower than ethanol's, so its attractions are weaker.
Ethanol has the largest molar mass but a smaller ΔHfus than water or ammonia.
6.01 kJ for ice versus 23.3 kJ for ammonia: boiling ammonia takes more.

items.q: A burn from steam at 100 °C is usually worse than a burn from the same mass of liquid water at 100 °C. Which explanation uses the table correctly?
options: Steam is at a higher temperature than boiling water, so it carries more energy to the skin.
Steam condensing on the skin releases 40.7 kJ/mol before the water even starts to cool.
Steam has a higher specific heat, so it releases 6.01 kJ/mol more as it cools.
Liquid water absorbs energy from the skin by evaporating, so it does not burn.

why.correct: Each mole of steam that condenses releases 40.7 kJ to the skin, far more than cooling the liquid by a few tens of degrees releases.
options: Both are at 100 °C; the difference is the energy released on condensing.
Right: condensation is exothermic, and its energy is added to the energy released as the water cools.
6.01 kJ/mol is ΔHfus, the energy for melting and freezing, not for condensing.
Hot liquid water does burn; it just releases less energy than steam.

items.q: Why does the temperature of a melting ice-water mixture stay at 0 °C while energy is added?
options: The added energy is lost to the room as fast as it is added.
The thermometer stops reading temperature changes while ice is present.
The added energy overcomes attractions between water molecules instead of speeding them up.
The added energy breaks O–H bonds inside the water molecules.

why.correct: During a phase change, energy goes into potential energy (separating molecules), not kinetic energy, so the temperature is constant until the change is complete.
options: In a sealed, insulated container, the temperature still stays at 0 °C until the ice is gone.
The thermometer works fine; the temperature really is constant.
Right: potential energy rises as the solid structure comes apart; average kinetic energy, and so temperature, stays the same.
The molecules stay intact as H₂O; only attractions between them are overcome.

items.q: How much energy, in kJ, is needed to turn 18.0 g of ice at −10.0 °C into liquid water at 25.0 °C? Use c(ice) = 2.09 J/(g·°C), c(water) = 4.18 J/(g·°C), ΔHfus = 6.01 kJ/mol and 18.02 g/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out melting. The flat part at 0 °C takes the most energy of the three steps.
Value: you used water's specific heat, 4.18 J/(g·°C), for the ice too. Split the 35.0 °C rise: ice from −10.0 to 0 °C with 2.09 J/(g·°C), then liquid from 0 to 25.0 °C with 4.18 J/(g·°C).

items.q: How many grams of ice at 0 °C can be melted by 5.00 kJ of energy? (ΔHfus = 6.01 kJ/mol; 18.02 g/mol)

mistakes.why: Value: that is moles of ice. Multiply by the molar mass for grams.
Value: you used ΔHvap. Melting uses ΔHfus.

items.q: A student heats twice as much of the same solid with the same heater. Predict how each quantity on the new heating curve compares with the original.

variables.name: Length of time of the melting plateau
variables.why: Twice the moles need twice the energy to melt, which takes twice the time with the same heater.

variables.name: Temperature of the melting plateau
variables.why: The melting point is a property of the substance, not of the amount.

variables.name: Molar enthalpy of fusion calculated from the data
variables.why: Twice the energy divided by twice the moles gives the same kJ/mol.

why.correct: Amount changes the energy (and time); the substance sets the melting temperature and the per-mole enthalpy.

items.q: A drink is cooled with either 50 g of ice at 0 °C or 50 g of liquid water at 0 °C. Which cools the drink more, and why?
options: The cold water, because liquid water has a higher specific heat than ice.
They cool it equally, because both start at 0 °C.
The ice, because melting it absorbs energy from the drink before the meltwater starts to warm.
The cold water, because ice releases energy as it melts.

why.correct: Melting is endothermic. The ice takes energy from the drink to melt (6.01 kJ/mol, about 334 J/g) and then more to warm, so it cools the drink more.
options: Both warm up from 0 °C, but only the ice also absorbs energy by melting.
Same temperature, but the ice must also melt, which absorbs energy.
Right: each gram of ice absorbs about 334 J just to melt, on top of the energy it absorbs warming up.
Melting is endothermic: it absorbs energy.

items.q: Liquid wax in a candle mold cools and solidifies at its freezing point. Which statement about the wax during freezing is correct?
options: The wax absorbs energy from its surroundings while its temperature stays constant.
The wax releases energy, and its temperature falls steadily the whole time.
The wax neither releases nor absorbs energy, since its temperature does not change.
The wax releases energy to its surroundings while its temperature stays constant.

why.correct: Freezing is the reverse of melting: q = −n × ΔHfus. The released energy comes from new attractions, not from slowing down, so the temperature is constant.
options: Absorbing energy at constant temperature is melting, the reverse change.
During freezing the temperature stays at the freezing point until the wax is solid.
Energy leaves the wax even though its temperature is constant.
Right: freezing forms attractions between molecules, which releases energy; the temperature holds at the freezing point.

items.q: A cooling curve for a pure liquid shows a flat part at 80.2 °C. A sample of the same liquid with twice the mass is cooled in the same way. Where is the flat part on the new curve?
options: At 80.2 °C, lasting about twice as long
At 80.2 °C, lasting the same length of time
At about 160 °C, lasting the same length of time
At about 40 °C, lasting about twice as long

why.correct: The temperature of a plateau identifies the substance; its length reflects the amount.
options: Right: the freezing point does not depend on the amount, but twice the mass releases twice the energy.
Twice the mass must release twice the energy to freeze, which takes longer.
Freezing points do not scale with mass.
The freezing point is a property of the substance, not the amount.
